subject: physiology
title: PAH Clearance, Effective Renal Plasma Flow, and Renin Release

steps.tx: Quantification of total renal plasma flow requires a substance that is almost completely removed from renal arterial blood in a single capillary transit. The exogenous organic anion **para-aminohippurate**, abbreviated as PAH, is freely filtered at the glomerulus and avidly secreted by proximal tubular basolateral transporters.
steps.say: Para-aminohippurate is filtered and avidly secreted, clearing nearly ninety percent of plasma in a single pass.

left.title: PAH Handling in Kidney
points: Freely filtered across glomerular capillaries (~20% of renal load)
Actively secreted by proximal tubule OAT transporters (~70% of load)
Approximately 90% extracted in a single circulatory pass
PAH clearance measures effective renal plasma flow (ERPF)

right.title: Inulin Handling in Kidney
points: Freely filtered across glomerular capillaries (~20% of load)
Zero tubular secretion and zero tubular reabsorption
Exactly 20% extracted in a single pass (matching filtration fraction)
Inulin clearance measures true glomerular filtration rate (GFR)

steps.tx: Because approximately ten percent of renal blood flows through non-clearing medullary capsules and adipose tissue, kidneys do not achieve one hundred percent extraction of PAH. Consequently, PAH clearance measures **effective renal plasma flow**, which averages roughly six hundred millilitres per minute in healthy adults.
steps.say: PAH clearance measures effective renal plasma flow, underestimating true renal plasma flow by about ten percent.

steps.tx: Active tubular secretion of PAH is a saturable carrier-mediated process relying on basolateral organic anion transporter 1 and apical multidrug resistance proteins. When plasma PAH concentration exceeds approximately twenty milligrams per decilitre, the **transport maximum for PAH** is reached, causing clearance to drop toward inulin clearance.
steps.say: When plasma levels exceed transport maximum, PAH secretion saturates, and its clearance declines toward inulin clearance.

steps.tx: Three structures meeting at one tubule corner run the kidney conversation with the arteriole. The **juxtaglomerular apparatus** joins macula densa cells sensing distal salt, granular cells storing renin, and the afferent arteriole they regulate. Low sensed salt releases renin and constricts the efferent side through angiotensin, defending filtration pressure. Most blood pressure pharmacology is an argument with this small apparatus conducted by tablets.
steps.say: The juxtaglomerular apparatus senses distal salt at the macula densa and releases renin to defend filtration. Most pressure drugs negotiate with it.

steps.tx: Endocrine regulation of systemic blood pressure and renal hemodynamics is anchored by the **juxtaglomerular apparatus**, located at the vascular pole of the nephron. It comprises three specialized structures: granular renin-producing juxtaglomerular cells in afferent arterioles, the sensor macula densa in the thick ascending limb, and extraglomerular mesangial lacis cells.
steps.say: The juxtaglomerular apparatus controls renin release through granular juxtaglomerular cells, the macula densa, and mesangial cells.

vis.caption: Juxtaglomerular apparatus anatomy, renin granules, and vascular microenvironment.

steps.tx: The proteolytic hormone **renin** is synthesized, stored, and secreted by specialized granular juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole. Renin release is triggered by three primary physiological stimuli: decreased renal perfusion pressure (renal baroreceptor), increased renal sympathetic nerve activity, and diminished sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa.
steps.say: Renin is released in response to low arteriolar perfusion pressure, renal sympathetic activation, or low sodium delivery.

rows: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors on JG cells
Low dietary salt, vigorous loop diuretic therapy

steps.tx: Unlike most secretory cells where calcium promotes exocytosis, renin secretion is uniquely inhibited by elevated intracellular calcium. Consequently, increased arterial stretch opens stretch-activated calcium channels, raising intracellular calcium and suppressing **renin release from granules**; conversely, low calcium or elevated cyclic adenosine monophosphate strongly triggers exocytosis.
steps.say: Uniquely, calcium inhibits renin secretion, meaning low intracellular calcium and high cyclic AMP trigger renin release.

nodes.label: Renal Hypotension or Sympathetic Beta-1 Stimulation
Intracellular cAMP Accumulates; Intracellular Ca2+ Suppressed
Granular Exocytosis Releases Active Renin into Renal Circulation
Renin Cleaves Circulating Angiotensinogen to Angiotensin I

steps.tx: Once in the systemic circulation, renin acts enzymatically upon liver-derived angiotensinogen, cleaving a decapeptide designated angiotensin I. Within pulmonary and renal capillary endothelium, **angiotensin converting enzyme** removes two C-terminal amino acids to generate the potent octapeptide vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, which stimulates arterial constriction and adrenal aldosterone release.
steps.say: Renin cleaves angiotensinogen into angiotensin one, which angiotensin converting enzyme converts into active angiotensin two.

Renin Cleaves Angiotensinogen (14-mer) into Inactive Decapeptide Angiotensin I
Endothelial ACE (Pulmonary and Renal) Converts Ang I into Active Octapeptide Ang II
Angiotensin II Drives Vasoconstriction, Aldosterone Secretion, and Na+ Retention

steps.tx: Rare renin-secreting juxtaglomerular cell tumors, or hemangiopericytomas, produce autonomous oversecretion of renin, causing severe hypertension and hypokalemia. Similarly, unilateral renal artery stenosis produces **secondary hyperreninaemic hypertension**, where local renal parenchymal ischaemia stimulates persistent excess renin output despite high systemic blood pressure.
steps.say: Renal artery stenosis triggers persistent renin secretion, producing severe secondary hypertension and hypokalemia.
